stem: A 54-year-old with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits 700 mL fresh blood. BP 84/50 mmHg, pulse 122/min and he is confused. He has ascites and previous oesophageal varices. His airway is currently patent.
ask: Which treatment bundle is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange outpatient gastroscopy in 7 days after oral iron replacement.
Give high-dose oral proton-pump inhibitor and monitor until morning.
Start vasoactive therapy and IV antibiotics promptly while resuscitating for urgent endoscopic therapy.
Give tranexamic acid as sole haemostatic agent before considering fluids or blood.
Place a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube immediately without discussing specialist airway protection.
explanations: Active major upper GI haemorrhage with shock mandates emergency resuscitation and endoscopy.
Acid suppression alone cannot treat suspected variceal bleeding or shock.
Correct: suspected variceal haemorrhage needs parallel resuscitation, portal-pressure reduction, infection prophylaxis and therapeutic endoscopy.
TXA is not recommended as routine treatment for GI bleeding and does not replace resuscitation or endoscopy.
Balloon tamponade is a temporary rescue for refractory haemorrhage with expert airway protection, not first-line.
pearl: In suspected variceal haemorrhage, give early vasoactive agent plus antibiotic prophylaxis while organising definitive endoscopic banding.
pivot: Non-variceal ulcer haemorrhage instead centres on endoscopic haemostasis and indicated PPI treatment, not routine terlipressin.

steps: Resuscitate and protect airway
Call critical care, gastroenterology and blood bank; ABC, IV access, crossmatch and blood products guided by physiology/coagulopathy.
Treat presumptive varices
Start terlipressin or somatostatin analogue and prophylactic IV antibiotics per local guideline; consider IV PPI until bleeding source confirmed.
Definitive haemostasis
Urgent endoscopy once appropriately stabilised for band ligation; consider rescue TIPS if recurrent/uncontrolled.
Observe closely
Serial BP, HR, Hb, urine output, encephalopathy and rebleeding; plan secondary variceal prophylaxis after recovery.
management.safety: Avoid reflexively transfusing to unnecessarily high Hb in portal hypertension; use specialist transfusion targets.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 46-year-old with diabetes has 24 hours of right upper quadrant pain, fever 38.8 °C, Murphy sign and WCC 17 × 10^9/L. Ultrasound shows gallstones, 5 mm gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid without bile duct dilation. BP is 118/72 mmHg.
options: Treat with oral antacids and discharge because gallstones are commonly incidental.
Start IV fluids, analgesia and appropriate antibiotics with early surgical review for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Perform ERCP urgently in all patients even without jaundice or common duct obstruction.
Observe without antibiotics or surgery until the pain resolves for six weeks.
Begin oral ursodeoxycholic acid as definitive emergency gallstone therapy.
explanations: Fever, Murphy sign and gallbladder inflammation indicate acute cholecystitis, not dyspepsia.
Correct: treat inflammation/infection and plan source control during the admission when suitable.
ERCP is for duct stones/cholangitis, not routine uncomplicated gallbladder inflammation.
Delaying treatment risks perforation, abscess and recurrent sepsis.
Ursodeoxycholic acid has no role as acute treatment of infected gallbladder inflammation.
pearl: Acute cholecystitis is usually managed with supportive treatment and early definitive cholecystectomy in an operative candidate.
pivot: If too frail or septic for surgery, percutaneous cholecystostomy may bridge to definitive treatment.

steps: Stabilise
NPO, IV fluids guided by status, analgesia/antiemetic, blood cultures if sepsis and assess organ dysfunction.
Treat
IV antibiotics covering likely biliary flora per local pathway and promptly involve general surgery.
Source control
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during admission if suitable; assess duct obstruction or cholangitis separately.
Monitor
Pain, fever, WCC, bilirubin/LFT, haemodynamics and postoperative complications.
management.safety: Ascending cholangitis or organ dysfunction changes urgency and may require ERCP-based biliary drainage.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 69-year-old presents with 8 hours of severe groin pain, vomiting and a previously reducible femoral swelling that is now tense and exquisitely tender. Skin is erythematous; HR 120/min, lactate 3.8 mmol/L and there are peritoneal signs.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Give laxatives and review after the bowel opens.
Use prolonged forceful manual reduction to avoid emergency surgery.
Arrange ultrasound in 48 hours because femoral hernias are rarely incarcerated.
Resuscitate, give indicated antibiotics and obtain immediate surgical exploration.
Discharge with a truss and plan elective mesh repair next month.
explanations: Obstruction and possible ischaemia require emergency surgical care, not bowel stimulants.
Forceful reduction can push ischaemic bowel into the abdomen and delay diagnosis of necrosis.
An irreducible painful femoral hernia with systemic signs is high risk for strangulation.
Correct: possible strangulation/peritonitis is a surgical emergency; imaging must not delay exploration.
A truss is inappropriate and unsafe in suspected strangulated bowel.
pearl: Painful irreducibility with systemic toxicity, lactate rise or peritonism suggests strangulation—not a hernia for routine reduction.
pivot: A soft reducible hernia without obstruction or systemic signs may be evaluated electively for repair.

steps: Resuscitate
NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV access, bloods including lactate/crossmatch, analgesia and NG tube if vomiting/obstructed.
Surgical response
Urgent general-surgery/anaesthetic evaluation and immediate operative exploration; give IV antibiotics when ischaemia/perforation suspected.
Definitive care
Reduce/repair hernia and resect nonviable bowel as required; postoperative monitoring for sepsis and ileus.
management.safety: Do not perform taxis when strangulation is suspected.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 60-year-old with a prior laparotomy has colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and no flatus for 24 hours. CT shows a transition point with dilated small bowel but no free gas, reduced enhancement, closed loop or pneumatosis. Vitals and lactate are normal.
ask: What is the BEST initial plan?
options: Keep NPO, resuscitate with IV fluids, decompress with NG tube as indicated and arrange serial surgical assessment.
Give stimulant laxatives and high-fibre meals to open the bowel.
Perform immediate laparotomy for every radiologically confirmed obstruction.
Discharge with antiemetics and return if still vomiting after 48 hours.
Give empiric high-dose corticosteroids as primary treatment.
explanations: Correct: stable uncomplicated adhesive obstruction can receive a carefully monitored non-operative trial.
Oral intake and stimulant laxatives increase aspiration/dilation risk in mechanical obstruction.
Surgery is needed for strangulation, peritonitis, complete unresolved obstruction or failed conservative trial, not every stable adhesive SBO.
Obstruction requires inpatient surveillance for ischaemia, fluid shifts and deterioration.
Corticosteroids do not relieve a mechanical adhesive transition point.
pearl: CT signs of ischaemia, peritonitis, closed-loop obstruction or failure to improve change management from supportive observation to urgent surgery.
pivot: If peritonitic, unstable or with CT closed loop/reduced bowel enhancement, proceed toward emergency operation rather than prolonged non-operative trial.

steps: Assess
NPO, ABC, abdominal exam including hernial orifices, IV fluids and electrolyte correction, strict input/output.
Decompress and image
NG decompression if persistent emesis/distension, review CT for transition and bowel viability.
Observe actively
Serial pain, tenderness, HR, lactate, urine output; senior surgery review and consider water-soluble contrast pathway if appropriate.
Escalate
Operate urgently for ischaemia/perforation/peritonism or unresolved obstruction after appropriate monitored trial.
management.safety: Avoid giving oral contrast to a patient with severe aspiration risk without appropriate precautions.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 73-year-old has fever 39.5 °C, jaundice, RUQ pain and hypotension. Bilirubin is 110 µmol/L, ALT elevated and ultrasound shows a 12 mm common bile duct with suspected distal stone.
ask: Which intervention should be prioritised once resuscitation begins?
options: Repeat ultrasound next month because duct dilation is often age related.
Perform laparoscopic cholecystectomy alone before treating the obstructed duct.
Give oral ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve the duct stone.
Observe on IV antibiotics alone until fever resolves, regardless of persistent obstruction.
Provide urgent biliary decompression, usually ERCP, in addition to IV antibiotics and shock resuscitation.
explanations: Charcot triad plus shock indicates severe cholangitis needing urgent source control.
Gallbladder removal will not urgently drain an infected obstructed CBD in shock.
This does not provide rapid drainage or infection control.
Antibiotics alone may fail when infected bile remains obstructed and needs source control.
Correct: severe cholangitis requires early antimicrobial therapy and urgent biliary drainage.
pearl: Ascending cholangitis = infection behind biliary obstruction. Definitive management is source control by duct drainage.
pivot: Uncomplicated symptomatic cholelithiasis without cholangitis is managed with elective/early cholecystectomy rather than emergency ERCP.

steps: Resuscitate
ABCDE, IV access, cultures, fluids with reassessment and vasopressors if septic shock persists.
Treat infection
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative bacteria and appropriate enterococci according to local policy.
Drain
Urgent gastroenterology/ERCP for biliary stent or stone extraction; percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP unavailable/failed.
After recovery
Arrange definitive gallstone management to reduce recurrence.
management.safety: Do not wait for full normalisation of LFTs or cultures before arranging drainage in severe cholangitis.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 25-year-old at 22 weeks gestation develops migratory periumbilical-to-right lower quadrant pain, focal tenderness and low-grade fever. Ultrasound cannot visualise the appendix. Maternal vitals are stable and fetal heart rate is present.
ask: What is the NEXT most appropriate step?
options: Discharge because pregnancy-related ligament pain explains right-sided discomfort.
Obtain MRI abdomen/pelvis without gadolinium and involve surgery/obstetrics.
Perform urgent contrast CT in every pregnant woman before senior review.
Give opioid analgesia then postpone evaluation until after delivery.
Perform immediate laparotomy without review or additional assessment solely because ultrasound was inconclusive.
explanations: Progressive focal pain and fever raise appendicitis concern; delayed diagnosis risks perforation.
Correct: after non-diagnostic ultrasound in a stable pregnant patient, MRI is a useful non-ionising diagnostic test.
CT can be used when necessary but is not automatically preferred when MRI is available and the patient stable.
Analgesia should not delay evaluation of potential surgical abdomen.
The clinical picture and availability of MRI/senior surgical review guide timing; a stable case allows rapid diagnostic refinement.
pearl: In pregnancy, appendicitis can have atypical anatomy; diagnostic delay raises perforation and preterm labour risk.
pivot: If generalised peritonitis or maternal instability is present, urgent surgery may supersede further imaging.

steps: Assess jointly
Senior obstetric and general surgery assessment, maternal observations, abdominal exam and fetal assessment.
Image promptly
Ultrasound first; MRI without gadolinium if non-diagnostic and available, or CT when clinically indicated and benefits outweigh radiation risk.
Treat confirmed disease
IV antibiotics and timely appendicectomy under surgical/anaesthetic planning, with perioperative fetal considerations.
management.safety: Do not withhold necessary surgery because of pregnancy; delay may pose a greater risk.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 21-year-old three hours after tibial shaft fracture fixation has escalating leg pain despite opioids. Toes are warm and pulses palpable. Passive extension of the toes causes severe pain; calf compartments feel tense.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Document palpable pulses and observe until the next ward round.
Increase opioid analgesia and apply a tighter compressive dressing.
Urgently notify orthopaedics, remove constrictive dressings and prepare for emergency fasciotomy.
Request routine outpatient nerve conduction studies in six weeks.
Elevate the limb well above heart level and use ice while waiting 12 hours.
explanations: Pulses often remain present early in compartment syndrome and do not exclude ischaemic damage.
Analgesia and compression mask or worsen dangerous compartment pressure.
Correct: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch after trauma are classic signs needing urgent decompression.
Neuropathy testing is irrelevant and dangerously delayed for threatened muscle necrosis.
Marked elevation can worsen perfusion; suspected compartment syndrome requires immediate surgical evaluation.
pearl: Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical time-critical diagnosis; present pulses or normal skin colour do NOT rule it out.
pivot: If findings are equivocal in a sedated/unreliable patient, compartment pressure measurement may help, but must not delay treatment of obvious disease.

steps: Recognise
Call orthopaedic surgeon immediately; check pain with passive stretch, sensation, motor function and compartment tension.
Remove pressure
Split dressings/cast, keep limb near heart level, give oxygen/support BP and analgesia without delay.
Definitive care
Emergency surgical fasciotomy and postoperative monitoring for rhabdomyolysis, renal injury and wound complications.
management.safety: Delay can cause irreversible myonecrosis and nerve injury within hours.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 46-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis and immunosuppressive therapy has a hot swollen knee, fever 38.6 °C and cannot bear weight. BP 120/70 mmHg. Bedside ultrasound shows a large effusion.
ask: What is the BEST initial approach?
options: Start intra-articular corticosteroid immediately because RA flare is most likely.
Treat with oral NSAIDs and arrange rheumatology review in two weeks.
Order MRI before obtaining a joint aspirate.
Arrange urgent aseptic synovial aspiration and blood cultures, then empiric IV antibiotics and orthopaedic drainage planning.
Prescribe oral doxycycline alone and reassess the swollen knee tomorrow.
explanations: Steroid injection into an infected joint can worsen infection; septic arthritis must be excluded.
Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage rapidly and needs emergency assessment.
MRI may be useful in complications but should not delay aspiration, cultures and treatment.
Correct: aspiration confirms infection and guides microbiology, while prompt antibiotics and source control protect joint and patient.
Empiric outpatient oral therapy is inadequate for a suspected infected native joint.
pearl: Septic arthritis is a joint emergency: aspiration before antibiotics is ideal if stable, but do not delay antimicrobials in sepsis.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable, start antibiotics immediately after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: First steps
Assess sepsis, give analgesia, contact orthopaedics, blood cultures and labs.
Sample
Aseptic joint aspirate for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals; crystals do not exclude concurrent infection.
Treat
Empiric IV antibiotics guided by local resistance and risk factors; urgent washout/drainage as required.
Follow
Tailor therapy to culture, repeat assessment for ongoing infection and rehabilitation when safe.
management.safety: Immunosuppression can blunt fever or inflammatory signs; maintain a low threshold for septic arthritis.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 49-year-old with a history of lumbar disc prolapse reports new urinary retention, bilateral sciatica, reduced perineal sensation and progressive foot weakness. Post-void residual is 800 mL.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Prescribe oral prednisolone and physiotherapy, with review after one week.
Arrange urgent MRI of the lumbar spine and immediate spinal surgical consultation.
Perform diagnostic lumbar puncture first to assess inflammatory neuropathy.
Reassure because preserved anal tone rules out cauda equina.
Give a suprapubic catheter and defer neurological evaluation until bladder function recovers.
explanations: Acute retention and saddle sensory loss are red flags of cauda equina compression; outpatient care is unsafe.
Correct: suspected cauda equina syndrome requires same-day imaging and assessment for urgent decompression.
LP is not first-line with compressive red flags and can delay or complicate treatment.
A single normal exam finding does not exclude evolving cauda equina syndrome.
Bladder decompression may be needed but does not treat the compressive emergency.
pearl: New urinary dysfunction plus saddle change with back pain is an emergency even if limb power and rectal tone are partly preserved.
pivot: For uncomplicated mechanical radicular pain without bladder/saddle red flags, analgesia, activity and conservative follow-up may be appropriate.

steps: Recognise
Urgent spinal/orthopaedic or neurosurgical referral, document lower-limb motor/sensation/reflexes, perineal sensation and bladder function.
Image
Emergency MRI lumbar spine; do not let delays in routine investigation or analgesia mask evolving deficits.
Support
Bladder catheter if retention, analgesia and prepare for urgent surgical decompression if compression confirmed.
Document
Careful timing of symptom onset, serial neurological examination and informed consent.
management.safety: A missed cauda equina syndrome can lead to permanent bowel, bladder and sexual dysfunction.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 24-year-old arrives febrile and confused with rapidly progressive headache, neck stiffness and petechial rash. BP is 98/58 mmHg. GCS 12; there is concern for raised intracranial pressure. Blood cultures can be drawn now, but CT and LP will take an hour.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next management?
options: Wait for CT and CSF microscopy before prescribing antimicrobials.
Arrange outpatient oral amoxicillin because bacterial meningitis rarely causes a petechial rash.
Perform lumbar puncture immediately despite altered consciousness and suspected raised ICP.
Give prophylactic antibiotics only to housemates while observing the patient.
Take blood cultures if feasible and give immediate empiric IV antibiotics with resuscitation and indicated dexamethasone per protocol.
explanations: Delaying antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis/meningococcaemia worsens outcomes.
This presentation indicates possible invasive meningococcal disease with sepsis requiring admission and IV therapy.
LP may be unsafe until airway, circulation and raised-ICP risk have been assessed; bloods and treatment should not wait.
Contact prophylaxis is important after diagnosis but does not substitute for the patient's emergency treatment.
Correct: prompt parenteral therapy should precede delayed CT/LP when bacterial meningitis is likely.
pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, do not delay IV antibiotics for imaging/LP when the procedure is unsafe or delayed.
pivot: If alert, stable and without contraindications, perform rapid LP promptly when it will not delay antimicrobial therapy.

steps: First minutes
Activate sepsis pathway, ABC, isolation if meningococcal risk, IV access, blood cultures and glucose.
Treat
Empiric IV meningitis antibiotics promptly per local age/risk protocol; consider dexamethasone before/with first dose when indicated.
Investigate safely
CT only when neurological/red-flag indications; LP once safe, with CSF culture/PCR and cell counts.
Prevent spread
Notify infection control/public health and give close contacts chemoprophylaxis according to guidance; monitor neurological sequelae.
management.safety: Do not perform LP in shock, active seizures, focal mass concern or significantly impaired consciousness without senior review.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.
